evidence_quotes.quote: More specifically, our empirical investigation is concentrated on the effect of the ZEIS implementation on the percentage of homeowners, the number of bathrooms per household, the percentage of households with access to garbage collection services, the percentage of households with access to piped municipal water, and the percentage of households with access to sewage services through the general network.

According to the legislation, five conditions are necessary for areas of low-income settlements areas to be eligible for ZEIS Status: have predominantly residential use, present an average household income equal to or less than three minimum salaries, have lack or absence of basic infrastructure services, have a housing density of no less than 30 residences per hectare, and be subject to urbanization. Urban land regularization involves adverse possession (usucapião), for private areas, or the Granting of the Right to Use (Concessão de Direito Real de Uso), in case of public land.
The process of demarcating an area as ZEIS demands a specific municipal law and a work of mapping and registering households, demanding, thus, municipal resources.

We thus explore the fact that it is possible to observe treated and non-treated eligible areas in a pre-intervention period (1991) and two post-intervention periods (2000 and 2010) and consider a difference-in-difference strategy (Angrist and Pischke, 2008).

On the other hand, according to the numbers of Panel B, we obtained a positive impact of about 19 percentage points of the ZEIS implementation on the percentage of households with access to sewage services through a public network

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household access to piped municipal water through the public/general network and access to sewage services through the public/general network (as well as mean bathrooms per household) across low-income urban settlements in Recife, Brazil.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: Clearly yes, as the study evaluates municipal urban zoning and land-regularization legislation (Social Interest Special Zones, ZEIS, enacted via Municipal Laws 14,511/83 and 14,947/87 PREZEIS and settlement-specific municipal laws). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Also yes (with minor borderline nuance noted because ZEIS operates as a settlement-level legal zoning and regularization regime that also prioritizes urbanization investments rather than a standalone utility tariff/connection rule). Specifically, ZEIS is an enacted legal-regulatory mechanism involving (1) statutory eligibility screening (five legal criteria including average household income <= 3 minimum salaries, residential predominance, density >= 30 residences/ha, and lack of basic infrastructure), (2) administrative household mapping and registration via specific municipal statutes, (3) tenure regularization instruments (usucapião on private land and Concessão de Direito Real de Uso on public land), and (4) differentiated urbanistic/lot-size regulatory accommodation incorporating informal settlements into formal municipal water and sewerage provision, rather than generic construction project delivery, behavioural promotion, or unanalysed macro-governance background.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary quantitative empirical analysis combining Recife municipal administrative/GIS records (PLHIS) on ZEIS statutory demarcation with temporally harmonized Brazilian Demographic Census tract panel data (1991, 2000, and 2010) using Propensity Score Matching and Difference-in-Differences regressions.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports census-tract percentage of households accessing piped water via the general public network, percentage of households accessing sewage services via the general public network, and mean number of bathrooms per household (alongside homeownership and garbage collection). Note: statistical significance and direction do not determine eligibility, though Tables 1-6 also provide full effect estimates and clustered standard errors suitable for quantitative synthesis.
criterion_notes.c5: Population/unit of analysis (temporally harmonized Demographic Census tracts in Recife, Brazil; baseline 19 [or 18] ZEIS-treated tracts with >90% coverage and 54 PSM-matched non-ZEIS control tracts across 1991, 2000, and 2010, N=219/216 tract-year observations, plus slum-control and coverage-threshold robustness samples), exposure (statutory ZEIS demarcation between 1991 and 2010), outcomes (piped water network connection %, public sewage network connection %, bathrooms/household), and quasi-experimental PSM-DiD study design are all clearly identified.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English (with bilingual English and Portuguese title and abstract), which is directly eligible without translation.

study_design: Quasi-experimental longitudinal panel study combining Propensity Score Matching (PSM) and two-way fixed-effects Difference-in-Differences (DiD) across 1991, 2000, and 2010 census tracts
population_and_sample: Temporally harmonized Demographic Census tracts representing households in low-income urban settlements in the City of Recife, Pernambuco, Brazil across 1991, 2000, and 2010 (962 citywide tracts; baseline sample of 19 ZEIS-treated tracts with >90% ZEIS area share [18 treated in 1993-1996 in dynamic models] and 54 Propensity Score Matched non-ZEIS control tracts, N = 219 [or 216] tract-year observations; robustness checks with 84 non-ZEIS slum tracts, N = 306, and 50%-100% ZEIS area share cutoffs)
exposure: Statutory demarcation and implementation of Social Interest Special Zones (ZEIS) under Recife municipal land-use and tenure-regularization laws (Municipal Laws 14,511/83, 14,947/87 PREZEIS, 16,113/95, 16,176/96, and settlement-specific municipal laws enacted between 1991 and 2010, predominantly 1993-1996)
outcome: Census-tract percentage of households accessing piped municipal water through the public/general network, percentage of households accessing sewage services through the public/general network, and mean number of bathrooms per household (alongside homeownership percentage and garbage collection percentage)
rationale: This full-text empirical study in English evaluates the causal effect of statutory demarcation of Social Interest Special Zones (ZEIS) in Recife, Brazil on census-tract access to piped municipal water via the public network, sewage connection via the public network, and bathrooms per household using Propensity Score Matching and two-way fixed-effects Difference-in-Differences across the 1991, 2000, and 2010 censuses. It satisfies all inclusion criteria (c1-c6) under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2, because ZEIS is a specific municipal legal regime establishing statutory eligibility screening, household mapping/registration, differentiated urbanistic/lot-size regulatory accommodation, and legal tenure regularization (usucapião and Concessão de Direito Real de Uso) to incorporate informal settlements into formal municipal water and sewerage networks.
